title: YJIT and Runtime Optimization
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of yjit and runtime optimization in a Ruby program and name the key rule involved.
Apply yjit and runtime optimization in a small example and predict its result before running it.
Identify one boundary or failure case related to workload-specific evaluation and verify the intended behavior.

content.intro: Learn YJIT and Runtime Optimization through a visual model, a minimal Ruby example, and a practical check.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding yjit and runtime optimization helps you write code that is easier to explain, test, and maintain. It also helps separate Ruby language guarantees from runtime assumptions, dependency behavior, and application-specific rules.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: YJIT and Runtime Optimization helps you reason about just-in-time compilation concepts. In Ruby, prefer a small example whose inputs and expected result are easy to explain. This lesson connects the syllabus topic to practical code and highlights where assumptions or edge cases matter.

content_blocks.title: How to think about it
content_blocks.text: Begin by identifying the key rule: Just-in-time compilation concepts. Then connect it to Supported runtime options. The remaining syllabus points—Measuring real-world effects, Workload-specific evaluation—are useful checks before applying this in a larger project.

content_blocks.title: Guided example
content_blocks.text: Run the example as written, compare it with the expected result, and explain why each line supports yjit and runtime optimization. Next change one input or condition and predict the result before running it.

content_blocks.title: Try it yourself
content_blocks.text: Create a second example for yjit and runtime optimization using a different input. Add one edge case from the syllabus list (Workload-specific evaluation), state the expected behavior, and write a small test or manual check that would catch a regression.

content_blocks.title: Run, troubleshoot, and reset
content_blocks.text: Save as lesson.rb and run `ruby lesson.rb` from a terminal. CodeLeaf currently has no isolated Ruby runner, so these examples should be run locally until one is deployed. If the command fails, confirm `ruby --version`, inspect the full error message, and verify that required standard-library or gem dependencies are installed. Reset by removing temporary files created by your experiment and returning the code to the smallest reproducible example.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain yjit and runtime optimization, identify its place in performance and memory management, run a focused example, and verify an important boundary. Revisit the linked exercise if this is a core topic; advanced runtime or framework examples remain draft until reviewed in a suitable environment.
